There are two articles about menopause in the the_bmj_ this week, and neither mentions hormone treatments.

The first is advice for doctors going through perimenopause. The advice is to change your shifts, protect your breaks and drink more water. Sorry what about hormone treatments to improve symptoms and enable people to work better?

If I stopped my progesterone, estradiol and testosterone, I would not be able to think clearly or remember drug doses for my patients. Before I started HRT and testosterone I was really struggling to work as a GP. Extra breaks wouldn't have helped my brain to function, but replacing the hormones I'm missing does.

The second article shows brain scans before and after menopause, with less grey matter in brains of menopausal women. It concludes that they still don't know what that means.

I do know thought and so should they. This is basic physiology. Hormones - progesterone, estradiol and testosterone - work in every cell in the brain, and when we don’t have them, our neurons fire differently, glucose metabolism drops, the cells don’t repair as well, as well as many other beneficial effects. 

The effects of these low hormones during menopause lead to symptoms including brain fog, lost words, anxiety and low mood that women describe to me in my newson.health clinic each day. 

So, in medicine we should always be trying to treat the underlying cause. I speak to many women who get their memory, focus and confidence back once their missing hormones are replaced.

Doctors read the BMJ to learn, and this issue was a missed opportunity to learn about perimenopause, menopause and hormones.

Compounded hormone treatments contain exactly the same progesterone, estradiol and testosterone as  bioidentical hormone treatments made by pharmaceutical companies, yet many doctors and clinicians dismiss them. 

Pharmacists have been making medicines for individual patients for centuries, and compounding is still used every day for many drugs including chemotherapy for cancer, drugs for neonatal care and in children's medicines. 

With compounded hormone treatments, the difference lies in the dose, the form and the base the hormone is mixed with. That can matter a great deal for women who don't absorb estradiol well from patches or gels, or who react to the colourings, fillers and preservatives in some licensed products.

Licensed HRT works well for many women, but some need a different dose, route or an additive-free preparation, and they deserve that choice. 

Quality can vary between compounding pharmacies. In my new article on my website, I've included the questions to ask your prescriber and your pharmacy, and I explain why you should never buy hormones online or use them without medical supervision.

Most clinicians receive very little training on compounding. If you're a healthcare professional, or you know one who needs to read this, please share it with them. Read the full article now via the link in my bio.

Testosterone isn’t only a male hormone. It is the most biologically active hormone in women.

Women have testosterone receptors in every cell of their body. Testosterone affects their brain, bones, muscles, mood, energy, memory and libido. When women are younger, their testosterone levels are higher than their estradiol levels.

Testosterone levels usually start to fall from the late 20s and early 30s and many women then notice symptoms without knowing why. They often feel exhausted, lose their motivation, struggle to concentrate, have aching muscles and joints, or lose interest in sex. Too often each symptom is treated separately, so many women are misdiagnosed with depression, personality disorders, fibromyalgia and chronic fatigue syndrome, when the cause underneath is never looked at.

Bioidentical testosterone, usually prescribed as a cream or gel, can be taken with HRT or on its own and it shouldn’t be so hard for women to access. There are so many unfounded fears and reservations of prescribing testosterone which are harming women. Leaving symptoms untreated has real consequences and this need to change.

One of the questions the three of us hear most from women is: “What can I do if I’ve been told no?”

A global survey of more than 3,500 women found over 60% had seen multiple healthcare professionals before getting hormone treatment. One in ten had more than ten GP appointments first. That’s not acceptable.

The “hormones” in contraception are not hormones.

I was chatting with Dr Val Pollard, who I trained with at medical school and who now works with me at newson.health, and we both admitted that for many years we prescribed contraception wrongly believing we were prescribing hormones, and we also thought that the progesterone-only pill was simply progesterone. It isn’t. 

Contraceptives contain synthetic progestogens and, in the combined pill, ethinylestradiol, and no cell in the human body produces progestogens or ethinylestradiol. They have completely different chemical structures to our own hormones and the natural, bioidentical hormone treatments we prescribe now, and these synthetic hormones are associated with risks, including risk of heart disease, clots and cancer. 

That’s why the blanket term HRT is so unhelpful, because it groups very different treatments together as though they’re the same. 

Language matters in medicine and women deserve to know exactly what they are being prescribed so they can make an informed choice and be educated about risks of each treatment.

Why are only around 5% of menopausal women prescribed HRT?

This week on my drlouisenewsonpodcast, Dr Jerrold Weinberg menopausemended, an obstetrician and gynaecologist who has practised medicine for 50 years, explained how we got here. When a woman stops making estradiol, the simple answer is to replace it, yet there are still unfounded fears about HRT. The first hormone treatments were made from pregnant mares' urine (Premarin) and the synthetic progestogen medroxyprogesterone acetate (Provera) which are associated with small risks. However, these are very different to the bioidentical hormone treatments we prescribe now which are not associated with these risks. However, there are a whole generation of doctors who have not been trained to prescribe hormone treatments.

The bioidentical hormone treatments, progesterone, estradiol and testosterone, which we prescribe now are the same structure as the hormones our bodies make and are therefore very different from the older types of HRT. Women who are prescribed the right dose and type of bioidentical hormone treatments often them feel like themselves again, as well as having better future health.

Every woman struggling with symptoms of hormonal changes, at any age, deserves the chance to make an informed choice about being prescribed hormone treatments.

“Too young”, “too old”, “too risky” to be prescribed hormone treatments…

Which is safer to prescribe to a menopausal woman with osteoporosis, a bisphosphonate or HRT?

I saw a woman in my newson.health clinic who is 62 and has been without hormones for 20 years, since her periods stopped at 42. No one considered hormone treatments then and she was told the risks were too high. Now she doesn’t want to take bisphosphonates because she’s read about their risks, yet she’s been told she has to. 

Her GP documented what he thought the risks of HRT are, including cardiovascular disease, stroke and breast cancer, but not that those risks relate to synthetic hormones rather than the body identical hormones we prescribe now. She was also offered an antidepressant for slightly low mood, even though SSRIs are associated with lower bone density, and she’s already worried about another fracture.

Estradiol, progesterone and testosterone work physiologically on bone, helping osteoblasts build it and reducing the osteoclasts that break it down. Women deserve a choice and the best evidence. It is not right to withhold hormone treatments - progesterone, estradiol and testosterone - when that is what they both need and want.

A woman who reaches 45 has a 1 in 5 lifetime risk of Alzheimer’s; for a man the same age it’s 1 in 10. Nearly two-thirds of people living with Alzheimer’s are women, and longer lifespans don’t fully explain that gap.

Lisa Mosconi (dr_mosconi), a neuroscientist at Weill Cornell, published a review in Neuron in 2026 arguing that the menopause transition may be a turning point for brain aging. It’s a review of existing studies, not a new trial, so read most of this as association rather than cause. Here’s what the human data show:

-Perimenopause: brain scans can already look different before your last period. Regions affected early in Alzheimer’s use less glucose for energy and some memory regions are slightly smaller; after menopause the differences grow, and on average scans show slightly more amyloid. (Much of that scan work was done in women at higher risk, with a family history or the APOE4 gene.)
-Brain fog: up to 62 percent of women in perimenopause and postmenopause report it, and testing confirms a modest dip in verbal learning and processing speed during the transition that holds up after accounting for hot flashes, sleep, and mood.
-Your history: age at your first period, pregnancy, preeclampsia, gestational diabetes, and postpartum depression all show up in this story. Your reproductive history belongs in your brain health conversation.
-FSH and LH: as the ovaries slow, these pituitary hormones rise and stay high after menopause. A few small studies in women link higher levels to more Alzheimer’s-related markers. 

The evidence is early; it’s also a reminder that this isn’t only about estrogen.

Hormone therapy started near menopause mostly showed no harm to memory and thinking in trials, but it hasn’t been shown to improve memory or prevent Alzheimer’s. The open question is for whom, when, and with which formulation.

Women’s brains deserve attention at midlife, not decades later.
Education, not medical advice.

Source: Mosconi L. The neurobiology of menopause: Implications for brain aging and Alzheimer’s risk. Neuron. 2026. doi:10.1016/j.neuron.2026.09.015

SNL’s “Sister” sketch hit so hard because it isn’t really satire; it’s the default long-term care plan in this country, and it runs on women’s unpaid time.

Of the 63 million Americans providing family care right now, 61 percent are women, and the average caregiver is 51: right in the window of menopause (AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving, Caregiving in the U.S. 2025). In dementia care, more than one in three caregivers is a daughter (Alzheimer’s Association, 2025).

The money shows it most clearly. A MetLife analysis of Health and Retirement Study data (2011) put the average lifetime loss for a woman caring for an aging parent at $324,044 in wages, Social Security, and pension, compared with $283,716 for men. Caregivers spend an average of $7,242 a year out of pocket, about 26 percent of their income (AARP, 2021), and in 2025 nearly half reported a major financial hit like taking on debt, stopping savings, or not being able to afford food.

Your body keeps a ledger too. In a six-year study published in PNAS in 2003, Janice Kiecolt-Glaser’s team found that IL-6, an inflammatory marker linked to heart disease, type 2 diabetes, and frailty, rose about four times faster in people caring for a spouse with dementia, and the rise didn’t slow even years after caregiving ended. That study looked at spouses; we don’t have the same data on midlife daughters caring for parents, and that’s a gap worth funding.

Now, this doesn’t mean caregiving itself will make you sick. The research points to strain: long hours, no help, no relief.

The system’s backup plan is your sister. Women deserve a real one. Paid family leave, respite care, and a clinician who asks who’s taking care of you. Send this to your sibling (you know which one).

Sources: AARP and National Alliance for Caregiving, Caregiving in the U.S. 2025. Alzheimer’s Association, 2025 Alzheimer’s Disease Facts and Figures. I was recently asked about the IUD with amitriptyline, and the way it was asked implied this was a bad thing. 

I had not heard about it, so I looked into it and there is indeed an IUD with levonorgestrel (standard) and amitriptyline that is under development. There is only animal data and a small phase 1 study. 

The hypothesis? As amitriptyline is used for chronic pain, putting it in the uterus might help with painful periods and pelvic pain. It is an interesting hypothesis, and we always want to be intellectually humble and consider biologically hypotheses. This is how science advances for women. 

There seems to be a a knee jerk reaction that unless it is hormone therapy it is hurting women and that antidepressants are wrong. On this menopause day, I want to challenge everyone to be intellectually curious and humble. We need to consider all the evidence. We need open minds to change when the science doesn’t support our beliefs. We need to understand there can be many paths to health. And over promising on hormone therapy does not undo historical neglect in medicine, in fact, it perpetuates it.

“How long should I stay on HRT?” is a question I get all the time. Many women worry if it’s even worth starting if they might have to stop soon after.

The truth is, there’s no “hard and fast” rule that you must stop after five years. It’s a very individual decision based on your own health.

Here is what we consider:

👉 Individual Assessment: We regularly weigh up if the benefits of staying on HRT outweigh any risks for you personally.

👉 Modern Safety: Using newer, body-identical HRT is a much safer option.

👉 Protective Benefits: When started during perimenopause or early menopause, HRT protects your bones and likely your heart and blood vessels too.

👉 Feeling Better: Most importantly, it helps you feel like yourself again.

The best approach is to have regular chats with your doctor to stay up to date with the latest guidance and ensure the best outcome for you.

Is there a link between HRT and Alzheimer’s? It’s a question I hear often.

While we are still learning, here is what the current data shows:

👉 Women make up two-thirds of Alzheimer’s cases.

👉 Oestrogen is very active in our brains.

👉 Brain imaging shows changes during menopause long before memory shifts occur.

👉 Longer lifetime exposure to oestrogen is likely protective.

👉 Early or surgical menopause without replacement may increase risk.

Deciding on HRT is about looking at the full picture of your individual health and benefits.

October is Breast Cancer Awareness Month, and this time last year I was starting my own breast cancer treatment. With follow-up scans and appointments this month, being back in those waiting rooms and waiting for answers has brought so much of that fear and health anxiety back.

there was a time when i genuinely wanted to crawl out of my own skin.

the anxiety was so unbearable that i literally wanted to be outside of my own body.

i was 37 when the anxiety and panic attacks began.

the smallest thing would set me off.

my husband could brake hard in traffic and i’d be beside myself. heart racing, body flooded with panic. it could take me 15 minutes to calm down.

i’d watch my children at their swimming lessons and imagine them drowning.

the phone would ring and i’d assume the worst.

someone’s hurt. someone’s ill.

i was catastrophising everything.

and the worst part? i knew it was irrational.

knowing that didn’t stop it.

it was like my brain couldn’t tell the difference between real danger and something that might happen. and my body reacted to both as though my life depended on it.

there were moments when i genuinely felt like something in my brain was going to snap.

writing this now, it sounds dramatic. but at the time, i felt like i was drowning in it.

and i had no idea perimenopause could be playing a part.

nobody had explained that oestrogen doesn’t just influence your periods. it also interacts with brain systems involved in mood, anxiety and our response to stress.

as oestrogen fluctuates in perimenopause, some women become more vulnerable to anxiety and panic. anxiety can have other causes, too, so new or severe symptoms deserve assessment.

but here’s what i wish i’d understood.

when your brain is constantly anticipating danger, you can start to lose trust in your own mind.

you question whether you’re coping, or whether this is just who you’ve become.

i wasn’t just frightened of what might happen to the people i loved.

i was frightened of what was happening inside my own head.

i spent so long wondering what was wrong with me, when what i really needed was to understand what was happening to me.

if this sounds familiar, please know there’s so much you can do to support yourself. and that’s exactly what i create content about.

follow whatthemenopause to understand what’s happening in your body and what you can do to feel like yourself again.

Before your feet hit the floor in the morning, gently wake up your joints.

Joints feel stiff in the morning because they’ve had relatively little movement overnight. Joint fluid distribution,  surrounding tissues and underlying conditions like osteoarthritis, inflammatory arthritis or menopause can all contribute.

Gentle movement can restore mobility, warm up the muscles and reduce the feeling of stiffness.

Video sped up. Move slowly and mindfully: 
1) Spread the fingers and rotate hands and feet five times in one direction and five times in the other direction

2) hug one knee to chest and hold for five breaths then hug the other knee

3) Placing feet wider than hips, drop both of knees  to one side then to the other side. 

4) Give yourself a full body stretch by reaching with the heels in one direction and the fingertips in the other

5) slowly make your way to a comfortable seated position and twist to one side stay there for five breaths then twist to the other side

6) seated cat cows mobilise the spine. Place your hands on your knees, inhale to lift the chest and look up at the ceiling then exhale rounding the spine and bringing your chin towards your chest 5 times.

To those of you in the US, happy Thanksgiving! I’m not typically one for gratitude lists, but if I made one this year, this community and your questions would be near the top (alongside coffee). Whether they land in my DMs or come up at the end of a talk, so many of them come back to the same thing: “OK, but what does this mean for me, at 52, training for my first 10K?” You don’t just want the research; you want to use it. That’s what fuels my work, and it’s a big part of why I have some exciting news to share today.

You're not a small man.

I’ve been battling the same problem my whole career. Most of the research behind how you train, eat, recover, and sleep wasn’t done on women; about 6% of sport and exercise science studies use exclusively female participants. The rest are done on men, or on mixed groups where women are underrepresented, and the results are rarely analyzed by sex. Then the findings get handed to us as though we’re small men. Spoiler: We’re not.

For years, I’ve translated what does exist into plain English for you through my newsletter, social platforms, hundreds of hours of podcasts, my books, and my courses. That isn’t going to change, but two things do keep coming up:

The research gap isn’t closing fast enough. New studies on women are coming out, but not at the pace we need, and not without funding.

You want more—more depth, more context, and answers that fit your age, your body, and your training. My current newsletter every two weeks can only go so far.

Science with Sims is my answer to both.

A percentage of every membership will go toward closing the research gap on women. That’s built into how this works from day one so that your membership helps to push this field forward.

And you get to put the science to use. As a member, you’ll get the latest research on active women, broken down and made actionable: what we know, what we don’t know yet, and what you can do about it now.

Comment SCIENCE to learn more.

When it comes to strength training, it's not just about lifting heavy (which I love to advocate!), it's so much richer than that. We see a big sex difference in dementia, Alzheimer's and cognitive decline in women as we age, and that can be exacerbated during perimenopause. Strength training is a big tool we can use to counter cognitive decline. Multiple studies have been released which point to how heavy load lifting stimulates neural conductivity improvement in the prefrontal cortex, which is primarily driving cognition. 

If you are new to lifting or are looking for further accountability in your journey, Power Happens is a strength training program I put together with Hailey Babcock that is built for women who are 40+ and want to enter or advance in their strength training journey.

One of the most overlooked effects of perimenopause is a drop in gut microbial diversity. Emerging research shows that the gut microbiome of postmenopausal women is less diverse and metabolically different from that of premenopausal women, largely due to the decline in estrogen and progesterone in late perimenopause. These hormone changes alter the gut’s “estrobolome,” the collection of bacteria involved in estrogen metabolism.

Lower diversity matters because the microbiome plays a role in so many things, from metabolic health and inflammation to body composition, bone density, and brain function. Studies show menopause-related microbiome changes are associated with higher waist circumference, blood pressure, and cardiometabolic risk markers.

This is one reason many women notice shifts in weight, energy, digestion, and mood during the menopause transition.

In my last newsletter, I wrote about perimenopause and menopause hormone therapy: how to spot the signs of perimenopause, how to find the right healthcare provider, and what to expect when you start MHT. Today, I’m picking up where I left off with the part I feel most strongly about: what active women should know and consider about MHT.

MHT is a tool, and a good one, but—as with so many things—lifestyle can be just as powerful (if not more so for some) and needs to be considered too. 

As I mentioned in Part 1, most experts now use the term MHT rather than HRT, because the goal isn’t to “replace” the hormones you once had. That distinction is the root of a lot of confusion.

The hormones in MHT don’t behave exactly like the ones your ovaries made. Treatment doses aim for a steady, low physiological level, not the higher pulses and rhythms of your natural cycle, and your body responds differently to them. So replacing some estrogen doesn’t mean restoring everything estrogen once did. 

How you take estradiol matters:

- Pills (oral) are processed by the liver before reaching the rest of the body, so much of the estradiol is converted to estrone, a weaker estrogen. The liver also makes more clotting proteins, which slightly raises the risk of blood clots. 

- Patches and gels (transdermal) absorb through the skin straight into the bloodstream, keeping a more natural balance of estrogens with little effect on the liver. 

MHT can ease menopausal symptoms and protect tissues like bone and the vaginal and urinary tract, but it isn’t a like-for-like replacement.

That’s why the research shows MHT is first and foremost a tool for symptom relief, with bone protection as its clearest long-term benefit. The literature doesn’t show it builds muscle, drives fat loss, or prevents heart disease (one major trial suggests it may slow early arterial changes when started soon after menopause, but that’s not the same as prevention). This is where the lifestyle levers like sleep, exercise, and nutrition really come to the fore.

Comment TWO to read the rest of my latest article on MHT. - Stace

You don't need to do everything at once. I want this to make starting out feel simpler, not harder! In summary, here’s where I'd advise starting:

1. Protect your sleep

2. Eat enough, and eat in sync with your day: prioritize protein, front-load your food earlier in the day to support your natural circadian rhythms, don't skip pre-training fuel, eat adequate carbs around training, and consider creatine supplementation.

3. Lift weights two to three times a week; do cardio you enjoy (limiting too much long, moderate-intensity training)

4. Manage your total stress load, training included

5. Build social connection and community into your life deliberately

Everything else can follow after these foundations are solid. And if you'd like more resources, comment PLAN to learn more.

After so many years of neglect and gaslighting, women are finally seeing unprecedented attention given to Menopause; with greater empowerment over the care for their menopausal symptoms. One such polarizing treatment is, of course, Menopause Hormone Therapy (MHT; also known as Hormone Replacement Therapy). (I won’t get into the full history of the pendulum swings of MHT prescriptions; but for those that are interested on the upswing until the Women’s Health Initiative and the misinterpretation of the study by the media, then the fear around the data, to the current popular media push for every menstruating individual to use MHT as a powerful anti-aging agent.)

Before I get a blaze of DMs and emails - I am NOT anti-MHT, but I am anti-rhetoric that hormone therapy is the be-all, end-all panacea that is being pushed around with misinformation. There are many alternatives to use that do not involve hormones and should also be considered.

Lifting weights is now recognized as good for more than “just” making muscle.

For decades, aerobic exercise was regarded as the primary form of exercise you should do for cardiovascular and other health benefits. Heck, that’s why endurance type exercise such as walking, biking, and running are commonly referred to as “cardio.” The physical activity guidelines have traditionally emphasized aerobic exercise for health, even though researchers have been talking about resistance training being good for your heart for more than twenty years.

“Resistance training not only can improve or maintain muscle mass and strength, but also has favorable physiological and clinical effects on cardiovascular disease and risk factors.” American Heart Association

Now, finally, the new American Heart Association (AHA) scientific statement in Circulation makes the argument that, “Resistance training not only can improve or maintain muscle mass and strength, but also has favorable physiological and clinical effects on cardiovascular disease and risk factors.”

The statement is an update from 2007, and summarizes the benefits of resistance training alone or in combination with aerobic training to improve traditional and non-traditional cardiovascular disease risk factors, especially since resistance exercise may be as effective as aerobic exercise for the prevention of chronic disease and improving health and lifespan.

​Read more >>> https://bit.ly/4hB8gmY or via link in bio!

Menopause hormone therapy (MHT) is one of the topics I’m asked about most, and the conversation around it has changed dramatically over the years. For two decades after the 2002 Women’s Health Initiative (WHI) study, women were told hormones were dangerous (which was largely a fault of media misinterpreting the design and results of the study). Now the pendulum has swung hard the other way, and if you believe everything you read on the internet you’d think every woman needs MHT, for life, or her health will fall apart.

The truth sits somewhere in the middle. MHT is a genuinely useful tool, and for many women it can be life-changing. But it isn’t a cure-all, and it doesn’t replace the lifestyle foundations that drive your health through midlife and beyond.

There’s so much to cover on this topic that I’ve split it into two parts. This week, we’ll cover recognizing the signs, finding the right provider, testing, and what to expect when you start. In my next newsletter on November 2, we’ll cover what MHT does (and doesn’t do) for your body, the testosterone question, non-hormonal options, and how long to stay on it.

An important note before we dive in: MHT is often also referred to as HRT (hormone replacement therapy) or simply HT (hormone therapy). They all describe the same treatment, but most experts now prefer MHT, because the goal isn’t to "replace" the hormones you previously had. It’s to ease symptoms and protect your health through this stage of life.

I’ve also asked my friend Dr. Kiki Silver to weigh in on some of the practical, in-clinic questions, since I am not a medical doctor. We’ve known each other since 2014, when we both lived in the Bay Area. Dr. Silver is a UCSF-trained internal medicine physician who sees women for menopause care, optimal aging, and athlete-specific health concerns. She’s also an accomplished endurance athlete.

We spend a lot of time talking about muscle, metabolism, and performance, but not nearly enough time talking about the brain. Yet women are disproportionately affected by cognitive decline and Alzheimer’s disease. Alzheimer’s is a brain condition that slowly damages memory, thinking, learning, and organizational skills. It is an abnormal buildup of amyloid and tau proteins that prevent neurons from working as they should.

There is not enough attention drawn to the fact that nearly two-thirds of Alzheimer’s cases are women, and women have a greater lifetime risk of developing the disease than men (the risk is 1 in 5 for women versus 1 in 10 for men). Women are often diagnosed later than men because the key memory tests doctors use rely on verbal skills—and women tend to do better on those, even in the early stages of decline. As a result, problems can be missed at first. But once symptoms do show up, women often decline more quickly, likely because they have a higher buildup of harmful tau proteins in the brain. This may be linked to differences in how women’s brains naturally clear out damaged cells and waste.

Although there is clearly a knowledge gap (as there is with so much of the health and fitness data women rely on), we can begin tracing the answers back to female biology, hormones, and how our brains respond to stress, inflammation, and aging across the lifespan. Let’s examine these factors more closely.

Train for the ​life ​you ​want​.

I want to zoom out and think about what a long peakspan actually looks like in practice. I know for me, it’s about still enjoying all of the sports and activities I know and love: riding my bike, swimming in the ocean with friends, hiking up a mountain, doing my favorite HIIT workouts. I also want to be able to carry my own groceries, chase after my grandkids, and get off the floor without thinking about it. And it’s not just physical—I want to remain cognitively sharp, emotionally resilient, enjoy time with my family and friends, and still have the capacity to do all of the things that make my life feel like my own. I'd invite you to think about the activities and pastimes you still want to enjoy too.

None of this will happen by accident—and none of it happens just because you ran a lot of marathons in your 30s and 40s.

As I continue to spend time with some of the latest longevity research, I see that building a training approach that is forward-looking is the only real way to safeguard your future. That approach needs to account for the specific vulnerabilities of your history, address the physiological realities of being a woman in perimenopause or post-menopause, and keep you strong, fast, and capable for decades. That’s the path to not just more years, but better ones.

Women respond differently to resistance training than men. We’re generally more fatigue-resistant, recover faster between sets, and often tolerate higher total training volumes. At the same time, gains in muscle mass can be slower, particularly if we're under-fueling, due to differences in muscle fiber behavior and anabolic signaling.

Hormones matter, but not in the rigid way they’re sometimes presented online.

Estrogen supports muscle repair, collagen synthesis, and neuromuscular coordination, which helps explain why some women may feel stronger or more powerful at certain times during their cycle. It also helps explain why we see a precipitous drop in power with an increase in soft tissue issues during perimenopause. However, responses are highly individual. Rather than prescribing training strictly by menstrual cycle phase (as we once used to), current best practice is to use individual symptoms, recovery, and performance feedback to guide when to push and when to pull back. Fixed calendar rules aren't supported by the evidence—and they're not how most women actually experience training.

For peri- and postmenopausal women, declining estrogen makes resistance training even more important for maintaining muscle quality, strength, and bone density. Heavy and explosive loading—appropriately progressed and well-fueled—remains one of the most powerful tools we have for long-term health and function.

I’ll be honest: more than once this week I’ve woken up and it’s taken me a moment to work out which city I’m in.

Highlights of the last few weeks include speaking at The epicenterofwomenssports in Portland, Oregon, for the Women’s Global Sports Summit; a quick trip across the Pond for the _thewellnessoasis in London (my first time speaking in the UK!); headlining the livelong_media Summit in New York City last weekend—and now I’m writing this on the plane to Massachusetts for the Level Up retreat. What’s different from when I started this work 25 years ago is that I’m now in rooms with people who can really help bring about lasting change—and that’s worth losing a little sleep for.

Perhaps life feels particularly crazy right now because my family and I have recently relocated to the U.S. and I’ve co-founded a new company (more on that below), so, err…you could say there’s plenty going on.

I love this work. Standing in a room full of women who are eager to understand their bodies, and watching their faces as things click, is exactly why I do what I do. But the stage is only half the picture.

The other half is being mom to a teenager who’s just started a new high school. I’m trying to be there for the wobbles and the wins, often from a hotel room (if you’ve ever attempted a meaningful conversation with a teenager at an inconvenient hour, you know it’s a skill).

I suspect many of you are carrying your own version of this: different details, that same feeling of holding a lot at once (and wondering if you can keep it all together).

Comment ROAD to learn more about what I've been up to lately, including a launch of a new company I co-founded, collectivexhealth plus how I generally try and hold it all together in the chaos. 

💛 - Stacy

You cannot build muscle and bone without abundance.

“That makes me really mad.”
“That hurt me.”
“I don’t agree with that.”
“No, I don’t want to do that.”

It’s telling the truth. Being authentic instead of agreeable. Instead of being the pleaser, the easy one, or the one who never wants to make a scene.

Because all of those things can actually be forms of suppression.

And although society may praise you for being “the easy one” or “the nice one,” your body won’t necessarily be praising you for it.

Chronic emotional suppression can contribute to stress and nervous system dysregulation, which is exactly why learning to recognize, feel, and honestly express your emotions can be such an important part of healing.

Sometimes one of the healthiest things you can do for your nervous system is simply tell the truth. ❤️

8 years ago, I had severe chronic pain in both feet and ankles.

I was diagnosed with tarsal tunnel syndrome, and not one, not two, but THREE orthopedic surgeons told me essentially the same thing: if I wanted to address the pain, I would need reconstructive ankle surgery.

I was told I needed orthotics. I was told there were structural problems that needed to be fixed. And I was told I would never walk without pain unless I had surgery.

I never had the surgery.

Today I have ZERO foot or ankle pain. I don’t wear orthotics. I don’t need special shoes. I walk, hike, golf, strength train and do whatever I want without thinking about my feet.

What changed?

I learned how pain *actually* works.

All pain is ultimately experienced through the brain. And some of the same brain networks involved in physical pain are also involved in stress, fear and emotional distress. When we’re chronically stressed or feel unsafe, the brain can become more protective and amplify pain.

Pain does not always equal damage. And a structural finding does not automatically mean that finding is why you hurt.

We also know that structural “abnormalities”—disc degeneration, bulging discs, arthritis, labral tears, tendon changes and more—are often found in people who have NO pain.

The finding can be real.
The pain can be real.
And the finding still may not explain the pain.

Chronic pain is far more complex than “something hurts, therefore something must be damaged and need fixing.”

For years, I believed my feet were the problem.

Then I learned the neuroscience of pain and began teaching my brain and nervous system that my body wasn’t broken and movement was safe.

Eventually, the pain disappeared.

No surgery.
No orthotics.
No pain.

8 pain-free years later, man am I glad I learned how pain actually works before I let someone reconstruct both of my ankles. 😵‍💫

If you live with chronic pain, please learn the neuroscience of pain.

It might just change your life too.

Because I didn’t realize my body was responding to what my brain expected to happen next.

For years, I believed every symptom meant something was wrong with me. Pain meant damage. Fatigue meant dysfunction. Gut issues meant something in my gut needed fixing. Every sensation sent me searching for another test, treatment, supplement, diagnosis or answer.

And without realizing it, I was teaching my brain the same thing over and over again:

Something is wrong.
My body isn’t safe.
Pay attention.
Protect me.

What finally changed everything for me was understanding that the brain isn’t simply responding to what is happening in the body. It is constantly making predictions based on past experiences, beliefs, fear, attention and what it expects to happen next.

This is part of what makes the placebo and nocebo effects so fascinating. Expectations can create measurable changes in symptoms and physiology—not because symptoms are imaginary, but because the brain and body are constantly communicating.

I had spent years expecting to be sick.

So I started teaching my brain to expect something different.

I stopped treating every symptom like an emergency. I stopped constantly checking, researching and fixing. I began giving my nervous system evidence of safety and intentionally practicing the expectation that my body was capable of healing.

And that was when everything began to change…

Your brain is always learning from what you repeatedly think, feel, focus on and do.

So one of the most powerful questions you can ask yourself is: What am I teaching my body to expect?

We’re living in a world where becoming highly offended has become the new norm.

Rather than walking around thinking there’s a problem with everyone else, I think every single one of us would benefit from healing the wounds within ourselves that contribute to why we’re so easily offended in the first place.

The world doesn’t change by constantly pointing the finger at everyone else.

Change always starts with us.

You deserve relationships and environments that help you grow, expand, and heal, not ones that continually drain you. ❤️
Don’t let hard stop you. Easy is always harder in the end. ❤️

I am crazy passionate about this topic because there are millions of people all over the world who do not have this knowledge, and they are suffering unnecessarily because of it.

They end up with chronic symptoms. Chronic pain, gut issues, anxiety, insomnia, skin issues, autoimmune issues, Lyme, chronic fatigue, IBS, tinnitus, and the list goes on.

And because they’re trying to be proactive and get to the “root cause,” they end up working with some type of root-cause practitioner who runs a ton of tests.

And guess what happens when you run enough tests? You find things.

Bad bacteria in the gut. Mineral imbalances. Parasites. Heavy metals. Mold. Lyme. Epstein-Barr. Hormone imbalances. Nutrient deficiencies. All of the things.

And then you take those findings and say, “There it is. THAT is why I’m not well.”

And folks, a finding does not automatically mean you’ve found the reason you’re symptomatic.

The sooner you understand that, the better, because otherwise you can do exactly what I did and spend years, and hundreds of thousands of dollars, chasing and trying to fix every abnormality somebody finds.

One of the most important things we have learned from the research is that many of these findings can also be present in people who are completely asymptomatic.

So then we have to ask a much better question:

Why does one person have debilitating symptoms while another person with the same finding feels completely fine?

It’s the state of the nervous system!

Your nervous system influences virtually every system in your body. Your immune system. Your gut. Your hormones. Your sleep. Your pain processing. Your inflammatory responses. Your heart rate. Your breathing. Your digestion. Your perception of internal sensations.

And when the brain and nervous system become sensitized and begin interpreting what is happening inside the body through a lens of threat, symptoms can become amplified and persistent.

And here is the part I am so passionate about: The search for the cause can quickly become part of the cause.

In a 2012 review, plastic surgeons Bryan Mendelson and Chin-Ho Wong mapped where the facial skeleton loses bone as we age. The eye socket opens up at its upper inner and lower outer edges, the midface recedes beside the nose and the jaw shrinks just in front of the jowl. The lower outer rim of the eye socket starts changing by middle age.

Dermatologist Dr. Doris Day sees these changes in her patients and addresses them in her practice.

Even if the skin looks healthy, the bone underneath can still change. The brow may lower, the eyes can appear smaller, and a treatment that worked at 20 might not be right at 50. Dr. Day adjusts where she uses Botox and fillers to match her patient’s current anatomy.

Skin goes through its own shift at menopause. Mark Brincat and his team found that women can lose up to 30% of their skin collagen in the first five years after menopause.

If you train hard or live in hot environments and sweat a lot, you are likely losing meaningful electrolytes in that sweat, particularly sodium. Sodium helps our bodies retain the water we drink. There are many factors that impact sweat losses so we can’t really make general recommendations, but it is something that should be taken seriously.

One RCT of 26 athletes showed they retained just 58% of plain water after exercise-induced dehydration. That rose to about 75% when drinking oral rehydration solutions or sports drinks, each providing some combination of sodium and carbohydrates.

Now, that doesn’t mean going overboard. Overhydration is a real thing, and diluting your serum electrolytes too much can cause all sorts of problems. Adding electrolytes to your water doesn’t eliminate this risk if your overall water intake is still too high.

None of this applies to short workouts assuming you are eating a normal diet (you may need to supplement if your natural intake of sodium is super low or you are dieting hard). If you engage in prolonged exercise though, especially in hot environments, adding electrolytes to your water is a smart move.

Most people backload their protein—light breakfast, light lunch, heavy dinner. But if your goal is muscle health, that’s a losing strategy.

To stimulate muscle protein synthesis (MPS), you need at least 2.5 grams of leucine per meal—typically found in 30–50 grams of high-quality protein. Your first meal breaks an overnight fast, when your body is catabolic and muscle tissue is especially vulnerable. Skip protein here (or skip the meal entirely), and you miss a critical opportunity to shift your body into an anabolic, muscle-preserving state.

This isn’t just a tip for older adults—sarcopenia starts long before you see it in the mirror.

The best defense is a proactive strategy: anchor your day with protein at breakfast and dinner, and combine it with consistent resistance training to protect muscle across the decades.

I did the maths on getting creatine from food so you don’t have to.

Harris et al found that a single 5g dose of creatine is equivalent to the amount in about 1.1kg of raw steak. That’s more than 2 pounds of beef a day. In reality of course no-one eats that much.

Plants don’t contain creatine and the research bears this out. In an 8 week training study, the vegetarians started off with lower muscle creatine levels than the meat eaters (117 vs 130 mmol/kg). After supplementation the vegetarians were able to increase their muscle creatine and lean tissue more than the meat eaters.

This is precisely what Harris found: those who started at the bottom end of the scale saw the biggest gains.

Research shows that 3 to 5g of creatine per day will keep your muscles saturated even on rest days. I take 5g every day myself. That’s a fundamental part of my regime.

As you get older the quality of your protein intake becomes a non-negotiable factor in the defence of skeletal muscle tissue.

Animal proteins provide a potent, highly bioavailable profile of the essential amino acids required for muscle protein synthesis. Most plant proteins fall short of this in terms of both concentration and essential amino acid profile (i.e. they are deficient in one or more of the essential amino acids) and as such are unable to adequately stimulate muscle adaptation. This is the very basis of the FAO’s digestibility coefficient for the essential amino acids.

Plant protein can certainly be part of the picture once you’ve established your daily intake with high quality protein. The marginal benefit of protein quality falls away once you’ve hit your minimum of 1.6g per kg of body weight. Some plant sources (soy in particular) are fairly good in terms of amino acid profile, the majority however are not very good for driving muscle protein synthesis.

Two recent clinical trials have looked at the effect of removing animal protein from the diet on muscle mass in older people.

In the first study, adults over 65 on a vegan diet for 12 weeks lost about 5% of thigh muscle volume, protein intake dropping to 0.8g/kg/day. Those on the vegan diet who also did strength training lost muscle too, just about half as much.

In the second study, adults over 55 who were doing resistance training three times a week and following mostly vegetarian diets saw an increase in muscle mass. Those who were eating some meat in their diet gained more muscle in their arms and legs and had a higher protein intake.

You can build muscle on a predominantly plant-based diet as long as your total protein intake is adequate and includes sources that provide all the essential amino acids required for muscle maintenance.

In a trial he helped design, dr.myohead matched a 4-ounce beef patty against a soy-based burger. He had to double the soy to roughly match the single beef patty in essential amino acids. The blood amino acid levels shocked him.

The back of a label just says protein, and that is extremely misleading. 

How much leucine is in that? 
How much methionine? 

Each of these amino acids has its own biological pathways and processes.

Glutathione production goes down as we age, and the need for methionine goes up. Older adults might need double to maintain it. If we don’t meet our protein requirements, which are set at an abysmal minimum, how do we keep up? Phenylalanine is needed for dopamine production too.

When we talk about protein as if it’s one thing, we aren’t telling the whole story.

Animal foods are roughly 45 to 50% essential amino acids. Plant foods? Closer to 35%. So, to match the equivalent EAA, how much more plant protein do you need to eat?

A lot more.

Don Layman’s math: with 100% animal protein, under 40 grams a day meets your essential amino acid requirements. Go vegetarian or vegan and, in his words, “you’re going to be approaching 120 to 130 grams of protein probably.”

People who go plant-based tend to lean on grains, he says. Beans and lentils make up only about 18% of plant-based protein, and the rest comes from “very poor quality” grains.
